headline: KP to launch six-year fiscal reform programme
summary: ISLAMABAD: Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, which remains structurally dependent on federal transfers, will launch a six-year World Bank-supported programme to strengthen its fiscal system and lay the foundation for improved service delivery.The World Bank is expected to approve a $200 million loan from the International Development Association (IDA) later this month to fund the programme’s expenditure framework for fiscal years 2027-32. The programme’s total financing is estimated at $650m, with the remaining amount to be provided by the KP government.Interventions related to taxation in the merged districts and former Provincially Administered Tribal Areas (Pata) are excluded from the Programme-for-Results (PforR) financing boundary because the provincial government has extended their tax-exempt status. The programme’s $20m investment project financing component will provide technical assistance in these areas.The primary beneficiaries of the Public Resources for Inclusive Development (PRID) Multiphase Programmatic Approach for KP are the province’s 41 million residents, who are expected to benefit from better-resourced and more efficient public services. Direct beneficiaries include recipients of improved healthcare and education services.World Bank is expected to approve $200m loan for revenue mobilisation, fiscal management and service deliveryTaxpayers and businesses, including more than 700,000 property owners, around 10,000 agricultural income taxpayers, and over one million vehicle owners, are expected to benefit from more transparent, service-oriented tax administration.In the health sector, an estimated 1.3 million people are expected to benefit from improved services at rural health centres. In education, better planning, budgeting and service delivery are expected to benefit about 3.7 million pupils enrolled in public primary schools across the province, including 2.1 million boys and 1.6 million girls.Private investors are expected to benefit from access to better statistics and improved tax administration services. More broadly, improved mobilisation of own-source revenue (OSR), stronger public financial management (PFM) and evidence-based policymaking and planning are expected to align resource allocation more closely with provincial needs, ultimately improving the quality and equity of public services and investment across KP.The province’s socio-economic outlook points to fiscal vulnerability and poor development outcomes. KP remains structurally dependent on federal transfers, while OSR finances a small and declining share of rapidly rising expenditure. Inflexible salary and pension obligations dominate spending, leaving less room for public investment.Since 2022, expenditure has risen due to higher salary and pension costs, the absorption of the merged districts, inflation, and an expanded Annual Development Programme (ADP), which also covers the salaries and allowances of contract and project staff. In fiscal year 2025, 35.3 per cent of the population lived below the national poverty line. About 40pc of children under five were stunted, 36pc of school-age children were out of school, and only 58pc were fully immunised.According to a document on the programme, the KP government has expanded the sales and property tax bases, improved taxpayer compliance and strengthened tax administration. Measures include digitising stamp duty and property tax records in 12 cities and partially integrating revenue databases.However, several constraints continue to hamper OSR mobilisation. These include a narrow tax base that leaves property, agriculture and large parts of the services sector outside effective taxation; fragmented revenue administration across three provincial agencies with overlapping mandates and limited data sharing; and inadequate digital capacity for registration, filing, assessment and enforcement.Published in Dawn, October 11th, 2026

headline: 50kg cement bag price rises by Rs201 in a year
summary: KARACHI: Construction costs have risen as cement manufacturers have increased prices by up to Rs201 per 50kg bag over the past year, according to official data released by the Pakistan Bureau of Statistics (PBS).According to the weekly Sensitive Price Index (SPI) for the week ending Oct 8, the average price of a 50kg cement bag stood at Rs1,596, compared with Rs1,395 in the week ended Oct 9, 2025, representing a year-on-year increase of 14.38 per cent.However, Topline Securities said in a report on Thursday that cement prices had increased by Rs100-150 per 50kg bag during the first quarter of FY27 compared with the same period last year, mainly due to higher fuel costs amid elevated international coal and diesel prices.Market sources said cement prices in Punjab were higher than those in Karachi.Higher international coal and diesel rates have contributed to rising production costsAdeel Ashraf of Topline Securities said Richards Bay coal prices averaged around $113.93 per tonne in 1QFY27, compared with $113.20 in 4QFY26 and $90.30 in 1QFY26.Sources said average coal prices had increased by around $20 per tonne on a year-on-year basis. Including freight charges, the average cost stood at $133 per tonne in 1QFY27, compared with $113 in the same quarter of the previous fiscal year.They estimated that the $20-per-tonne increase in coal costs translated into an additional cost of at least Rs20 per cement bag, while higher diesel prices added around Rs15 per bag.Despite these cost increases, sources said the overall increase in cement prices had widened manufacturers’ margins, potentially generating substantially higher profits in FY27.They warned that rising cement prices would further hurt ordinary citizens already struggling to afford expensive homes and flats. According to the sources, property investors continued to drive demand for housing projects, while houses and apartments remained beyond the reach of many ordinary buyers.The sources said cement manufacturers should have increased prices by only Rs50-70 per bag in response to rising coal and diesel costs.They also criticised regulatory authorities for failing to address the issue effectively. They said the Competition Appellate Tribunal had yet to decide a 2008 case involving alleged cement cartelisation, even after 18 years.Mr Ashraf said the listed cement sector was expected to post a combined profit of Rs32.4 billion in 1QFY27, compared with Rs27.8bn in 1QFY26, representing an increase of 16pc year-on-year and 16pc quarter-on-quarter. The year-on-year growth in earnings was primarily attributable to higher net sales amid increased retention prices.Net sales were projected to reach Rs143bn in 1QFY27, up 25pc year-on-year and 14pc quarter-on-quarter, driven by higher cement prices and growth in domestic dispatches. Local cement dispatches increased by 8pc year-on-year in 1QFY27, while export dispatches declined by 11pc. On a quarter-on-quarter basis, domestic cement dispatches rose by 9pc on the back of stronger demand, while export dispatches increased by 10pc.Published in Dawn, October 11th, 2026

headline: International Monetary Fund borrowers face debt strain
summary: WASHINGTON: Nearly half of the countries eligible for concessional financing from the International Monetary Fund (IMF) are either in debt distress or at high risk of it, while their interest payments have quadrupled since 2013, Transparency International (TI) says.In a report released ahead of the IMF and World Bank Annual Meetings in Bangkok from Oct 12 to 18, the anti-corruption organisation warns that secrecy and corruption in sovereign borrowing can also leave future generations paying for loans that benefit the powerful.The report urges governments and international lenders to make public borrowing more transparent, strengthen safeguards against corruption and give borrowing countries a greater say in decisions that shape their debt obligations.The report highlights the growing pressure on public finances in low- and middle-income countries. According to the report, at least 8 per cent of government revenue across these economies goes toward servicing debt. In Africa, 57pc of the population lives in countries that spend more on interest payments than on health, education and climate action.TI highlights interest payments have quadrupled since 2013The figures underline the difficult choices governments face as they struggle to finance essential public services while meeting obligations to creditors.But TI argues that the problem is not simply how much countries borrow. The terms under which loans are negotiated, the disclosure of financial agreements, and how borrowed money is used also determine who benefits and who ultimately bears the cost.“Without robust safeguards and effective controls over how loans are negotiated and managed, sovereign loans are misused and embezzled, enriching public officials and their cronies at the expense of future generations,” the report says.Opaque agreements and weak oversight can make it hard for citizens, parliaments, and independent watchdogs to determine who approved a loan, how much a country owes, and whether borrowed funds were used for their stated purposes.A critical moment in BangkokTI argues that the Bangkok meetings offer an opportunity to turn concerns about debt transparency and corruption into concrete policy commitments.The annual gatherings bring together finance ministers, central bank governors and leaders of international financial institutions, alongside business representatives and civil society organisations. The G20 finance ministers and central bank governors will also meet on Oct 15, providing governments with an opportunity to establish political priorities on debt transparency and accountability.Transparency International identifies several steps it wants these institutions to take.First, governments should end secrecy surrounding sovereign borrowing. It calls on G20 countries to require bilateral creditors and private lenders operating within their jurisdictions to disclose complete, transaction-level financial and non-financial information about public debt.The G20, working with the IMF and World Bank, should also develop common standards to limit confidentiality clauses in sovereign lending agreements. Such agreements, the report argues, should be consistent with borrowers’ access-to-information rules, including requirements for proactive disclosure and the legal consequences of withholding information.Published in Dawn, October 11th, 2026

WASHINGTON: Nearly half of the countries eligible for concessional financing from the International Monetary Fund (IMF) are either in debt distress or at high risk of it, while their interest payments have quadrupled since 2013, Transparency International (TI) says.

In a report released ahead of the IMF and World Bank Annual Meetings in Bangkok from Oct 12 to 18, the anti-corruption organisation warns that secrecy and corruption in sovereign borrowing can also leave future generations paying for loans that benefit the powerful.

The report urges governments and international lenders to make public borrowing more transparent, strengthen safeguards against corruption and give borrowing countries a greater say in decisions that shape their debt obligations.

The report highlights the growing pressure on public finances in low- and middle-income countries. According to the report, at least 8 per cent of government revenue across these economies goes toward servicing debt. In Africa, 57pc of the population lives in countries that spend more on interest payments than on health, education and climate action.

TI highlights interest payments have quadrupled since 2013

The figures underline the difficult choices governments face as they struggle to finance essential public services while meeting obligations to creditors.

But TI argues that the problem is not simply how much countries borrow. The terms under which loans are negotiated, the disclosure of financial agreements, and how borrowed money is used also determine who benefits and who ultimately bears the cost.

“Without robust safeguards and effective controls over how loans are negotiated and managed, sovereign loans are misused and embezzled, enriching public officials and their cronies at the expense of future generations,” the report says.

Opaque agreements and weak oversight can make it hard for citizens, parliaments, and independent watchdogs to determine who approved a loan, how much a country owes, and whether borrowed funds were used for their stated purposes.

TI argues that the Bangkok meetings offer an opportunity to turn concerns about debt transparency and corruption into concrete policy commitments.

The annual gatherings bring together finance ministers, central bank governors and leaders of international financial institutions, alongside business representatives and civil society organisations. The G20 finance ministers and central bank governors will also meet on Oct 15, providing governments with an opportunity to establish political priorities on debt transparency and accountability.

Transparency International identifies several steps it wants these institutions to take.

First, governments should end secrecy surrounding sovereign borrowing. It calls on G20 countries to require bilateral creditors and private lenders operating within their jurisdictions to disclose complete, transaction-level financial and non-financial information about public debt.

The G20, working with the IMF and World Bank, should also develop common standards to limit confidentiality clauses in sovereign lending agreements. Such agreements, the report argues, should be consistent with borrowers’ access-to-information rules, including requirements for proactive disclosure and the legal consequences of withholding information.

KARACHI: The Pakistan Stock Exchange (PSX) remained volatile during the outgoing week as escalating geopolitical tensions, elevated international oil prices and rising bond yields offset optimism over Pakistan’s Staff-Level Agreement (SLA) with the International Monetary Fund (IMF).

The benchmark KSE-100 index fell 0.6 per cent week-on-week to close at 167,089 points, shedding 1,066 points, according to Arif Habib Ltd (AHL).

Market sentiment remained subdued amid attacks on key shipping routes, with Yemen’s Houthis expanding their targets to Saudi Arabia’s civilian infrastructure and energy facilities. Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian refineries and concerns over US energy supplies also kept Brent crude above $100 a barrel, according to AKD Securities Ltd.

Index loses 1,066 points in outgoing week as Brent futures remain above $100 a barrel

The SLA on the fourth review of the Extended Fund Facility (EFF) and the third review of the Resilience and Sustainability Facility (RSF) provided some support. The agreement paves the way for disbursement of $1.2 billion under the two programmes, subject to approval by the IMF Executive Board. Total disbursements under the two programmes would reach about $5.7bn.

However, concerns over the widening trade deficit, inflation and the future interest-rate trajectory continued to weigh on investors.

According to AHL, the government raised Rs381bn against a Rs350bn target in its latest Pakistan Investment Bonds (PIBs) auction. Cut-off yields rose by 26-41 basis points across three-, five- and 10-year tenors, while the two-year yield declined by 19 basis points. Bids for 15-year bonds were rejected. The yield rise fuelled expectations of a possible policy rate hike at the next monetary policy announcement.

Pakistan’s foreign exchange reserves held by the State Bank of Pakistan rose by $15m to $21.5bn as of Oct 2. The rupee appreciated marginally by 0.03pc to close at Rs277 against the dollar.

Central government debt stood at Rs82.95 trillion at the end of August, up 7.1pc year-on-year but down 0.5pc month-on-month.

Sector-wise, banks were the biggest drag on the benchmark, shedding 566 points, followed by fertiliser companies with 234 points, automobile assemblers with 97, cement companies with 75 and textile composite firms with 43 points.

Habib Bank, MCB Bank and United Bank were the largest negative contributors, collectively accounting for 388 points of the decline. Fatima Fertiliser and Fauji Fertiliser Company also weighed on the index.

Oil marketing companies led positive contributions, adding 110 points, followed by power companies with 36 points. Pakistan State Oil was the largest individual contributor, adding 113 points, while Hub Power Company, Pakistan Oilfields, Engro Holdings and Mari Energies also supported the market.

Trading activity weakened during the week. Average daily volume fell 18.6pc week-on-week to 427 million shares, while the average traded value stood at $67m, down 2pc.

In the cement sector, despatches rose 6pc year-on-year to 4.62 million tonnes in September, supported by a 7pc increase in domestic sales, while exports remained flat. In the first quarter of FY27, despatches rose 4pc to 13.14m tonnes, with local sales up 8pc despite an 11pc decline in exports.

Banking sector deposits increased 14pc year-on-year to Rs39.2tr at the end of August, AKD Securities said. Cotton arrivals rose 5pc to 3.2m bales during September.

Oil production fell 6.4pc week-on-week to 63,700 barrels per day, while gas output declined 1.4pc to 2,999 million cubic feet per day, mainly because of lower production from northern oilfields and the Mari, Sui and Sharf fields.

Petrol prices increased 2.1pc to Rs398.96 per litre, while high-speed diesel prices fell 0.9pc to Rs395.72.

Elsewhere, Sindh Engro Coal Mining Company is expanding its Thar Block-II mine to supply additional coal to Lucky Electric Power Company, potentially enabling a complete transition to local coal and reducing reliance on imports.

Looking ahead, analysts expect quarterly earnings announcements and geopolitical developments to shape market sentiment. The index was trading at a 7.5x price-to-earnings ratio, with a dividend yield of 6.7pc.

They said easing inflation, improving economic indicators and any de-escalation in the Middle East could moderate oil prices and strengthen the case for monetary easing. However, persistent geopolitical uncertainty could continue to constrain gains.

article_text:
The apparent transformation of rural society sits uneasily with the landed elite’s strong presence in Pakistan’s legislatures, pointing to a disconnect between landownership patterns and political representation.

Does this reflect limitations in the sample-based Agriculture Census, ambiguities in legislators’ self-declared professions, or the disproportionate political influence of a relatively small landed class? How does this group continue to outnumber — and potentially outmanoeuvre — other professional categories in assemblies?

Across national and provincial legislatures, landowners and those with agri-business interests emerged as the largest professional group, based on members’ self-declarations to the Election Commission of Pakistan. This contrasts sharply with the changing rural landscape: official data show increasingly fragmented landholdings, with barely three per cent of farmers owning more than 12.5 acres.

Understanding legislators’ composition, backgrounds, and interests is essential to assess political and economic policy choices objectively. In Pakistan’s complex, multi-ethnic society, however, a vast informal sector, weak data collection, public mistrust and misreporting make this difficult. Limited access to official records has further constrained systemic research.

Many political leaders belong to the 3pc of farmers holding more than 12.5 acres

The Free and Fair Election Network (Fafen) Parliament Monitor on the 15th National Assembly 2018-2023, based on Election Commission of Pakistan (ECP) data, is perhaps the most comprehensive study of legislators’ professional backgrounds. According to Fafen, a similar analysis of the current legislatures is under preparation but has been delayed by the ECP’s slow provision of legislators’ declarations. Repeated attempts to seek the ECP’s input for this article were unsuccessful.

Of the total 1,058 legislators in the 2018 National Assembly and four provincial assemblies, 432 declared agriculture as their profession, far exceeding 223 businessmen, 81 full-time politicians, 49 lawyers, 25 doctors and 19 educationists, among others. Agriculturists accounted for 172 of 330 members of the National Assembly, 131 of 371 in Punjab, 76 of 168 in Sindh, 32 of 124 in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and 21 of 65 in Balochistan.

Shahid Khaqan Abbasi, former prime minister, businessman and senior leader of Awaam Pakistan, attributed the apparent disconnect to elite capture. “Members of the national and provincial assemblies, senators and political leaders largely belong to the 3pc of farmers holding more than 12.5 acres. They use their influence to control additional ‘benami’ land registered in the names of relatives, employees, servants or haris, secure government land on lease and obtain private land on concessional terms for cultivation by tenants.

“More importantly, many elite farmers derive substantial income from corruption and undeclared or illegal businesses, using agriculture income to launder earnings and evade taxes,” he alleged. “Besides, actually a large part of our elite uses ‘farming income’ to avoid taxes. The government does not ask how X acres of land can generate RsY of income. Everybody you meet will tell you, I have a ‘farm’. These are basically expensive, palatial homes built on farmland, and used to justify ‘farm’ income.”

Mr Abbasi argued that agricultural income also provides a convenient tax shelter for the wider elite. “Nobody questions how a given acreage can generate a declared level of income. Almost everyone claims to own a farm, often a palatial residence built on agricultural land, which is then used to justify supposedly agricultural earnings.”

Ziad Bashir, CEO of Ideas and a prominent business leader, argues that the apparent contradiction between 97pc of farmers operating less than 12.5 acres and agriculture dominating legislators’ declared professions may reflect different realities. Genuine fragmentation occurs through inheritance, while the census captures operational holdings, including tenancies, rather than simply ownership. But formal records may also understate effective control when family members or associates divide land while managing it as a single farm.

“Technology could help test this. Satellite imagery can identify adjoining parcels that show common cropping, irrigation, and harvesting patterns. Overlaying these with digitised land records and, under appropriate legal safeguards, ownership, family, utility, credit and crop-payment data could reveal who actually controls an agricultural operation. The constraint is therefore less technological than institutional: improving land records, data integration, transparency and political commitment.”

Dr Usama Ehsan Khan, an IBA researcher, stated that the apparent contradiction reflects two different measures. The Agriculture Census captures farm structure, overwhelmingly dominated by small holdings, while Fafen records legislators’ self-declared professions, revealing nothing about acreage owned. The real divide, therefore, is between the numerical dominance of small farmers and the disproportionate political influence associated with landed wealth.

Tax policy reinforces this dynamic. Agricultural income, taxed provincially, has historically enjoyed lighter taxation than comparable non-agricultural income, although recent reforms seek greater parity. Weak enforcement, combined with unequal landownership, patronage and access to state institutions, helps sustain landed influence despite continuing fragmentation of farms through inheritance.

Mehmood Nawaz Shah, president of the Sindh Abadgar Board, said the apparent disconnect raises two issues: the reliability of the census data and the fact that even if only 3pc of farmers own larger holdings, that pool is still sizeable enough to account for the strong presence of agriculturists in the assemblies.

A Lahore-based expert argued that agriculture has historically provided a convenient avenue for income-tax avoidance in Pakistan. Despite provincial legislation to tax agricultural income, enforcement remains weak, compounded by poor documentation of farm output and productivity.

Citing some 17,000 farms of 100 acres or more, he pointed to absentee landlords who lease land in smaller parcels to tenants or contractors. He argued that such earnings should be taxed like other rental income but often escape scrutiny. Shared ownership further complicates matters when one family member manages the entire holding without declaring the proceeds as personal taxable income.

Independent analyst Rashid Chaudhry argued that legislators often declare agriculture as their profession for tax advantages, although declining profitability makes it unlikely to be their principal income source. He said cotton’s collapse, repeated crop losses, and market crashes have undermined farming’s commercial viability.

Calling the sample-based Agriculture Census merely indicative, Mr Chaudhry questioned how much land the largest 3pc actually control, noting that land reforms remain stalled and individual holdings face no effective ceiling.

headline: Agriculture: Opting for sustainable farming
summary: A small farmer, Mohammad Siddique Channa from Balochistan’s Lasbela district, seems contented since switching to organic cotton cultivation under organic agriculture (OA) practices. Our land is still virgin while soil in Sindh and Punjab face degradation, but we do depend mostly on rain-fed irrigation, “ he said. They commonly borrow cash from private lenders in rural areas to keep their economic cycle going, then sell the harvest at a lower price to repay loans against inputs, with urea and DAP as major components.About $1.9 per kg was earned as foreign exchange, and $0.9m as carbon credits between 2016 and 2024 in the organic cotton projectThe Economic Survey of Pakistan 2025-26 puts fertiliser’s share in the cost of production of major crops at 10-15 per cent. Farmers spend Rs1.2 trillion annually to buy fertiliser. A Rs100 increase in the price of a 50kg bag adds Rs20 billion in financial burden to farmers’ pockets nationally.OA has emerged as a viable option for lessening the burden of synthetic fertiliser use worldwide, and it is being pursued as a global movement. In Pakistan, Balochistan province seems to be leading OA practices, primarily in cotton. The provincial government passed its Balochistan Organic Policy in Nov 2024 to promote OA by involving 12,000 farmers in collaboration with WWF-Pakistan under a project.OA helps achieve sustainable agricultural practices that support biodiversity, reduce reliance on fertilisers, pesticides, and imported seeds, and ensure economic growth. Under global OA practices, growers were encouraged to use natural inputs to produce nutritious organic food while protecting the environment.As Pakistan’s largest but least developed province, Balochistan accounts for 44pc of Pakistan’s landmass.“We initially started with 219 acres under a foreign-funded project in Lasbela, Sibi and Barkhan districts in 2016,” said Dr Syed Habibullah Shah, Director Balochistan Agriculture Extension and recipient of Sitara-e-Imtiaz. He deals with OA practices in specific districts of the province.In 2019, Pakistan produced its first organic cotton bale in Balochistan, a turning point that propelled the province into the global organic cotton cultivation arena. Experts like Dr Yusuf Zafar, former chairman of the Pakistan Agricultural Research Council, noted that although organic cotton holds a marginal 1.5pc share of global cotton production, demand is on an upward trajectory. The global organic cotton market was valued at approximately $3.25bn in 2026 and was projected to expand to $50.78bn by 2034. Among 28 organic cotton-producing countries, he explained, India alone accounts for a huge 51% of global organic cotton production.Organic cotton acreage in Balochistan has now reached nearly 133,257 acres across Kohlu, Barkhan, Khuzdar, and Lasbela districts. Balochistan produced the first regenerative cotton bale in 2024. Now, Washuk, Kharan, and Dera Bugti districts are being selected for organic cotton production.Different textile/ginners groups now sponsor organic farmers in organic cotton cultivation there. They provide non-GMO seed and other necessary inputs and pay a quality premium to producers, over and above the per-40 kg seed cotton price, after a duly verified process involving third-party validation by an international certification body, i.e., Control Union.“About 159,000 organic cotton bales are produced and marketed in Balochistan from an organic 89,000 acres that are globally certified in 2025. This bio-fertiliser, with more nutrients, improves water-holding capacity and soil OM, according to Mashood Siddiqui, a private company official working with Balochistan farmers.Textile millers find considerable potential for domestic organic cotton production, which was 2pc-3pc of total cotton. Organic cotton acreage in Balochistan has now reached nearly 133,257 acres across Kohlu, Barkhan, Khuzdar, and Lasbela districts. Balochistan produced the first regenerative cotton bale in 2024. Now, Washuk, Kharan, and Dera Bugti districts are being selected for organic cotton production.

Different textile/ginners groups now sponsor organic farmers in organic cotton cultivation there. They provide non-GMO seed and other necessary inputs and pay a quality premium to producers, over and above the per-40 kg seed cotton price, after a duly verified process involving third-party validation by an international certification body, i.e., Control Union.

“About 159,000 organic cotton bales are produced and marketed in Balochistan from an organic 89,000 acres that are globally certified in 2025. The registered organic area reached 133,257 acres. The differential certified area between 133,257 and 89,000 is undergoing the certification process,” Dr Habib said, quoting the summary of organic cotton in FY26. He claimed that since Balochistan doesn’t have many ginning units, cotton bale numbers from Balochistan were usually reflected in other provinces, including Punjab and Sindh.

He explained that Rs1.21bn (as per the project’s calculations) was paid to farmers as a quality premium in cash and kind. At the same time, $1.9 per kg was earned as foreign exchange and $0.9m towards carbon credit value between 2016-2024 in the organic cotton project.

Farmers are told how to collect animal dung and urine under a protocol. When it turns into compost, they apply it to the soil along with recommended tillage. This bio-fertiliser, with more nutrients, improves water-holding capacity and soil OM, according to Mashood Siddiqui, a private company official working with Balochistan farmers.

Textile millers find considerable potential for domestic organic cotton production, which was 2pc-3pc of total cotton. They argued that overall cotton crop production must reach 15m bales, up from the current 7m. It could potentially take textile exports from $19bn to $35bn annually.

• Pakistan Textile Exporters Associ­ation cites weak Western demand, higher freight, rising production costs• Exporters seek 6-8pc Duty Drawback of Local Taxes and Levies support, clearance of outstanding refunds• Industry says announced 4.5pc Export Finance Scheme rate yet to be implemented

ISLAMABAD: Textile exporters have warned the government of a steep decline in goods exports during the second quarter (October-December) of the current fiscal year, citing weakening demand in Wes­tern markets, rising freight charges and escalating production costs.

In a statement issued on Sunday, Pakistan Textile Exporters Associ­ation (PTEA) Patron-in-Chief Khur­ram Mukhtar said the country’s export sector was facing mounting pressure from multiple directions, threatening its competitiveness and share in international markets.

He said inflation in Western markets had weakened dem­and from international buyers, while sea freight charges had increased by 1.5 to 2.5 times, squeezing exporters’ already thin profit margins.

Rising input and logistics costs were further undermining the competitiveness of Pakistani products, he added.

“The decline in export trade volume is unprecedented,” Mr Mukhtar said, warning that only financially strong exporters would survive the prevailing conditions. He cautioned that regaining lost market share would be extremely difficult.

He said declining exports were affecting the entire textile value chain, including ginning, spinning, weaving, processing and knitting. The situation had been compounded by weak domestic demand amid high inflation, putting several segments of the industry under severe financial pressure.

Mr Mukhtar urged the government to provide temporary support thro­ugh the Duty Drawback of Local Taxes and Levies (DLTL) scheme at a rate of 6pc to 8pc to help exporters ret­ain their international market share. He also demanded immediate clearance of outstanding refunds under various heads to ease the liquidity crisis across the textile supply chain and called for the removal of cross-subsidies embedded in industrial energy tariffs to reduce production costs.

Highlighting anomalies in the Export Finance Scheme (EFS), he said the government had announced a fixed financing rate of 4.5pc in the FY27 Finance Bill, but the decision had yet to be implemented.

According to him, banks were charging exporters a minimum of 5.5pc, while some were charging as much as 8.5pc, contrary to the announced rate.

Mr Mukhtar claimed that around Rs200 billion in financing had been extended under the EFS to yarn exporters despite yarn being on the scheme’s negative list. He also questioned the provision of financing to sugar exporters, describing sugar as a highly regulated sector.

In contrast, he said, eligible textile exporters whose export performance exceeded the State Bank of Pakistan’s mandatory requirement by a substantial margin were being denied financing allocations.

He said some exporters were achieving five to six times the requi­red export performance against the mandatory threshold of two times, yet were unable to obtain financing.

Such allocations, he argued, discouraged value addition and penalised exporters contributing significantly to the country’s foreign exchange earnings.

Mr Mukhtar welcomed the incre­ase in EFS financing allocations for small and medium enterprises (SMEs) but questioned whether the additional funds could be effectively utilised.

He said an additional Rs300bn allocation for SMEs would require export performance of Rs600bn, which, according to him, did not currently exist. He pointed out that the Rs100bn allocation for SMEs in the previous fiscal year had lapsed without being utilised. He urged the government to review the distribution of EFS financing according to the export contribution of each segment, arguing that the top 100 exporters accounted for up to 60pc of total export volume and should receive proportionate financing.

To strengthen the textile supply chain, Mr Mukhtar proposed a targeted financing pac­kage of Rs140bn for modernisation and technological upgrading of four major segments.

The proposed package incl­udes Rs20bn each for ginning and sizing, and Rs50bn each for weaving and processing.

He said these sectors required specially designed short- and long-term financing facilities for balancing, modernisation and replacement of machinery, improving productivity and introducing automation and sustainable production practices.

Mr Mukhtar said the federal government and the State Bank should jointly develop the proposed financing programme in consultation with industry representatives.

He also called for a 10-year strategic plan for textile exp­orts, focusing on Pakistan’s exis­ting industrial expertise, exportable surplus and structural reforms needed to impr­ove international competitiveness.

“Historically, we have been reactive. The current situation demands a proactive appro­ach,” he said, warning that timely intervention would cost considerably less than efforts to recover lost export markets.

• FPCCI urges Nepra to reject inflated, disputed claims; flags previously disallowed, unverified adjustments• Demands detailed written responses, participation in public hearings• Discos claim Rs2.64tr in revenue requirements for CY2027

ISLAMABAD: The Federation of Pakistan Chambers of Commerce and Industry (FPCCI) has opposed an additional Rs268 billion burden on consumers sought by former Wapda distribution companies (Discos) through prior-year adjustments inpower tariffs.

In a comprehensive representation, the country’s top business body, representing large and small businesses, including manufacturing industries, asked the National Electric Power Regulatory Authority (Nepra) to reject the “inflated claims” previously disallowed by the regulator or disputed by third parties.

The representation follows tariff petitions filed by 10 Discos seeking adjustments to the indexation of multiyear tariffs (2025-30) for calendar year 2027 and other consumer-end tariff adjustments.

Collectively, the Discos have claimed Rs2.64 trillion in revenue requirements for CY2027 on account of distribution and supply of power.

The FPCCI said it had constituted a special Energy Advisory Committee (EAC) to review tariff filings, including claims related to working capital, power purchase prices, prior-year adjustments (PYAs) and returns on revenue base.

The committee found that Discos were seeking to pass hundreds of billions of rupees in prior-year adjustments on to consumers.

It said a substantial portion of these claims was retrospective, contested by third parties or previously disallowed by Nepra. Some claims were inconsistently calculated against the Discos’ own formulas or lacked sufficient disclosure for independent verification.

The EAC reviewed all 10 Discos’ CY2027 indexation and PYA petitions, including financial statements and annexures, on behalf of FPCCI’s constituent chambers, trade and industry associations.

According to the FPCCI, Islamabad Electric Supply Company’s (Iesco) PYA claims exceeded 212 per cent of its proposed annual margin, while Sukkur Electric’s claims amounted to 113pc of its distribution margin.

Faisalabad Electric’s PYA claims amounted to 91pc of its distribution and supply margin, followed by Multan at 68pc and Quetta at 60pc.

The corresponding shares for Lahore, Peshawar and Gujranwala electric companies stood at 41pc, 40pc and 32pc, respectively. Tribal Electric did not disclose the figures.

“These are not routine formula-based true-ups and ought not to be approved as such,” the FPCCI said.

The representation included itemised objections for each Disco and a cross-company comparison, identifying disputed amounts, grounds for objections and proposed disallowances based on petitions, financial statements and annexures published by Nepra.

The FPCCI demanded that its objections be made part of each Disco’s tariff-setting process, including public hearings, and that the companies respond in writing to specific objections before the hearings.

It also urged Nepra to reject undifferentiated lump-sum PYA claims, require component-wise substantiation and allow trade and business bodies to participate in hearings.

Faisalabad Electric has sought Rs535bn in revenue requirements for 2027, including Rs57bn in PYAs. The FPCCI called for rejecting Rs26bn in claims involving 11-year post-retirement benefits and previously disallowed supplementary charges.

Gujranwala Electric sought Rs70.4bn, including Rs17bn in PYAs linked to 19-year-old Azad Jammu and Kashmir sovereign receivables. Sukkur Electric claimed Rs68bn, including Rs36bn in PYAs.

Lahore Electric sought the highest revenue requirement, Rs759bn, including approximately Rs33bn in PYAs. The FPCCI said Rs27bn in claims were liable to be rejected because they had not been verified.

Iesco submitted the largest PYA claim of Rs158bn within its Rs525bn revenue requirement. The FPCCI said 70pc of Iesco’s PYA claims were either disputed or involved noncash items, had been filed as a lump sum and should be rejected.

Peshawar Electric sought Rs233bn in revenue requirements, including Rs35bn in PYAs. Of these, Rs33bn related to seven-year-old input tax claims that the FPCCI described as inadmissible.

headline: The influencer economy relies on advertisers borrowing the influencer’s credibility
summary: https://www.dawn.com/news/2036550
relevant_sector_or_market: AUTOMOBILE | ECONOMY & MACRO | MISCELLANEOUS | TECHNOLOGY & TELECOM
article_text:
The advertising business in Pakistan is undergoing a fundamental change. For decades, marketing was relatively straightforward. A company launched a product, appointed an advertising agency, produced a television commercial, bought airtime, put up billboards and perhaps hired a celebrity as its brand ambassador. The consumer has moved.

The advertising rupee is beginning to follow. Pakistan now has around 80 million adult social-media user identities. TikTok alone has an advertising reach approaching 80m adults, while YouTube reaches around 54m and Instagram around 22m. More importantly, Pakistanis are spending increasing amounts of their media time on these platforms.This has created a new industry: the influencer economy.

Consider the numbers. Jannat Mirza has over 25m followers on TikTok. Ducky Bhai has over 10m YouTube subscribers. Rajab Butt’s family channel has around 9m. Hania Aamir has crossed 20m followers on Instagram.

There are then thousands of smaller influencers specialising in fashion, food, beauty, technology, travel, gaming, automobiles and financial services. Why should companies care?

Content creators themselves will become businesses employing videographers, editors, and sales teams

Because advertising has historically been about renting somebody else’s audience. A brand paid a television channel because the channel had viewers. It paid a newspaper because the newspaper had readers. It paid for a billboard because people drove past it.

An influencer also owns an audience. The difference is that the relationship with that audience can be considerably more personal. If a television commercial tells me a restaurant serves excellent food, I know I am watching an advertisement. If someone whose food reviews I watch every week visits the restaurant and recommends a particular dish, the communication is different. The advertiser is effectively borrowing the influencer’s credibility.

Influencers get paid in several ways. The simplest is a fixed payment for a post, reel or video. Smaller influencers may receive a few thousand rupees or simply free products. Established creators can charge tens or hundreds of thousands of rupees. Celebrity influencers can command considerably more.

But the more interesting models are performance-based. An influencer can receive a commission for every product sold through a unique link or promotional code. Instead of paying Rs1m for an advertisement and hoping consumers buy the product, the company can pay according to actual sales.

Thus, advertising is becoming measurable distribution. Imagine a clothing company working with 100 influencers. Each receives a different promotional code. Within days, the company knows that influencer A generated 500 sales, Influencer B generated 50 and Influencer C generated none. The next marketing budget practically allocates itself. This also changes the economics for small businesses.

A new Pakistani cosmetics brand cannot compete with multinational spending but it can identify 50 beauty influencers whose followers match its target customer, send them products and compensate them partly on sales.

It also explains why follower count is becoming less important. An influencer with 50,000 followers interested in motorcycles may be more valuable to a motorcycle manufacturer than an entertainer with 5m followers. The question is not how many people follow you. It is whether they are the people I want to sell to — and whether they buy.

The next stage is live commerce. China has demonstrated how powerful the combination of influencers, entertainment and e-commerce can become. The influencer does not simply advertise a product. He or she demonstrates it live, answers questions, creates urgency and allows the customer to purchase immediately.

Pakistan has most of the ingredients required: smartphones, social media, digital payments, e-commerce logistics and, most importantly, a young population comfortable buying through a screen. An influencer can therefore move from being an advertiser to becoming a retailer. However, there are risks.

The first is transparency. Consumers frequently cannot distinguish between an independent recommendation and paid promotion. If an influencer is compensated that relationship should be disclosed. This becomes particularly important when influencers promote financial or health products. Trust cannot become a substitute for consumer protection.

The second problem is fake influence. Followers can be purchased, views can be generated, and engagement can be manufactured. Companies therefore need to stop measuring influencer marketing primarily through followers and start measuring it through customer acquisition cost, engagement, conversion and repeat purchases.This will also professionalise the industry.

Pakistan will increasingly see influencer agencies, talent managers, analytics companies, affiliate networks and technology platforms connecting brands with creators. Influencers themselves will become businesses employing videographers, editors, researchers and sales teams.

Traditional advertising will not disappear. Television remains powerful, billboards work, celebrity endorsements will continue, but the monopoly has disappeared. A Pakistani with a smartphone can now build an audience larger than many traditional media properties without owning a television station, printing press or an advertising agency.

And once you own the audience, you own something advertisers want. Pakistan’s next important retail channel may not be a shopping mall, television station or e-commerce website. It may simply be someone you follow.

The writer is the Chairman of the Pakistan Fintech Network

The government is looking to push for the privatisation of five to six entities that could raise upwards of $1 billion, Finance Minister Muhammad Aurangzeb toldReuterson Monday, stating that he expected the economy to grow by more than 4 per cent this fiscal year despite elevated oil prices.

Pakistan’s economy is considered to be highly vulnerable to a prolonged Middle East conflict given its dependence on Gulf energy imports, remittances and financing support from the region, even as it remains reliant on external financing to bolster foreign exchange reserves and meet debt repayments.

Pakistan has been able to procure adequate quantities of fuel, successfully avoiding any shortages, and critical sectors such as agriculture were holding up, Aurangzeb said.

“So I’m still quite clear that we should clock north of4pc,” he said in an interview on the sidelines of the annualmeetingsof the International Monetary Fund and World Bank in Bangkok.

“And on the inflation side, obviously, we are keeping a very close eye because it does have a knock-on impact in terms of the commodity prices.”

Following a period of severe economic turmoil exacerbated by the Covid-19 pandemic, the cash-strapped economy has recovered some of its footing, supported by a $7bn, 37-month IMF loan program known as the Extended Fund Facility signed in 2024 that includes some tough measures such as raising tax revenue on farm income.

Following theprivatisationof flag carrier Pakistan International Airlines last year, Aurangzeb said the government has around another dozen entities in the pipeline, including state-owned power distribution companies and the outsourcing of airport operations.

“I expect about five or six of these to go through during this fiscal year,” he said, adding that they could raise more than $1bn.

Privatisation has been seen as a key test of Pakistan’s reform credibility with the IMF, with officials previously underlining that failure to offload loss-making state firms risked renewed pressure on public finances.

“We are quite clear that we want the private sector to lead the country,” said Aurangzeb. “So our role is to help support, assist any way we can in terms of the ecosystem.”

The US-Israeli-ledwarwith Iran, now in its eighth month, and the inflation and hardship it has caused, will dominate the agenda and sideline conversations during the meetings that are being held outside Washington for the first time in three years.

Pakistan, whichreacheda staff-level agreement with the IMF last week, potentially unlocking about $1.21bn in financing under the Extended Fund Facility and a climate program, is continuing discussions with the United States for a proposed $10bn exchange stabilisation facility, Aurangzeb said.

But he declined to provide a time frame for the conclusion of negotiations.

“If it comes through, this will be a great help for us,” he said, referring to the facility, which is in addition to ongoing talks with the Export-Import Bank of the United States and the US International Development Finance Corporation.

“If it doesn’t come through, this does not, you know, create any problem for us in terms of access to market.”

headline: Americans Hall and Woodford win economics Nobel for stabilisation models
summary: Americans Robert Hall and Michael Woodford were awarded the Nobel economics prize on Monday for their work on how monetary and fiscal policy can better stabilise disruptive economic fluctuations.The two were honoured for developing new models for managing recessions and other crises that fail to respond to traditional tools.“On the basis of these models, well-timed fiscal and monetary policy measures can reduce the economy’s peaks and troughs,” the jury said.The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences explained in a statement that ever since John Maynard Keynes formulated his economic theories almost a century ago, “stabilisation” policies had long let officials boost economic growth when needed.But during the oil shocks in the 1970s, the Keynesian models that governed when and how action should be taken no longer worked.Hall, 83, a professor at Stanford University, and Woodford, a professor at Columbia University born in 1955, separately began to explore new models.“Rather than basing the models on statistical links between macroeconomic variables, such as inflation, production and consumption, they chose to build them on a microeconomic foundation,” the jury said.Hall and Woodford’s models include an “understanding for how the total mass of individual households and businesses affect the economy through their actions”, it said.A fundamental aspect of this is the understanding that households are forward-looking when making decisions about spending or saving.This means the way governments and central banks communicate their policies can influence people’s views of the future when making such decisions.The sign for the Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences in the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences ahead of the announcement of the 2026 Nobel Prize in Economics in Stockholm, Sweden, on October 12, 2026. — ReutersStable foundation“The laureates’ work has provided us with a stable theoretical foundation for the models that are now used by central banks and governments around the world,” John Hassler, chair of the Committee for the Prize in Economic Sciences, said in a statement.“It’s a surprise, but I’m feeling very good about it,” Woodford told reporters via phone during the announcement of the prize, saying he felt “elated” for receiving “a tremendous honour”.While his theories have had a large impact on policymakers, he said they had not been “motivated by a specific political agenda”.“It was an attempt to improve the foundations for discussion of economic policy and therefore to contribute both to the management of the economy, but also to contribute to public understanding,” Woodford said.The economics prize is the only Nobel not among the original five created in the will of Swedish scientist Alfred Nobel, who died in 1896.It was instead created through a donation from the Swedish central bank in 1968.But like the Nobels inchemistryandphysics, the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences chooses the winner and follows the same selection process.Last year, theeconomics awardwent to American-Israeli Joel Mokyr, France’s Philippe Aghion and Canada’s Peter Howitt for research into how technology drives and affects article_text:
Americans Robert Hall and Michael Woodford were awarded the Nobel economics prize on Monday for their work on how monetary and fiscal policy can better stabilise disruptive economic fluctuations.

The two were honoured for developing new models for managing recessions and other crises that fail to respond to traditional tools.

“On the basis of these models, well-timed fiscal and monetary policy measures can reduce the economy’s peaks and troughs,” the jury said.

The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences explained in a statement that ever since John Maynard Keynes formulated his economic theories almost a century ago, “stabilisation” policies had long let officials boost economic growth when needed.

But during the oil shocks in the 1970s, the Keynesian models that governed when and how action should be taken no longer worked.

Hall, 83, a professor at Stanford University, and Woodford, a professor at Columbia University born in 1955, separately began to explore new models.

“Rather than basing the models on statistical links between macroeconomic variables, such as inflation, production and consumption, they chose to build them on a microeconomic foundation,” the jury said.

Hall and Woodford’s models include an “understanding for how the total mass of individual households and businesses affect the economy through their actions”, it said.

A fundamental aspect of this is the understanding that households are forward-looking when making decisions about spending or saving.

This means the way governments and central banks communicate their policies can influence people’s views of the future when making such decisions.

“The laureates’ work has provided us with a stable theoretical foundation for the models that are now used by central banks and governments around the world,” John Hassler, chair of the Committee for the Prize in Economic Sciences, said in a statement.

“It’s a surprise, but I’m feeling very good about it,” Woodford told reporters via phone during the announcement of the prize, saying he felt “elated” for receiving “a tremendous honour”.

While his theories have had a large impact on policymakers, he said they had not been “motivated by a specific political agenda”.

“It was an attempt to improve the foundations for discussion of economic policy and therefore to contribute both to the management of the economy, but also to contribute to public understanding,” Woodford said.

The economics prize is the only Nobel not among the original five created in the will of Swedish scientist Alfred Nobel, who died in 1896.

It was instead created through a donation from the Swedish central bank in 1968.

But like the Nobels inchemistryandphysics, the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences chooses the winner and follows the same selection process.

Last year, theeconomics awardwent to American-Israeli Joel Mokyr, France’s Philippe Aghion and Canada’s Peter Howitt for research into how technology drives and affects growth.

Last week, South African judgeNavi Pillaywon the peace prize, and Canadian-Icelandic writerAnne Carsonwas named the literature laureate.

The Nobel Prize in Chemistry wasawardedto Frenchman Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai of Japan, and the Physics Prize to BelgianFrancis Halzen.

And the first prize to be announced, inmedicine, went to American Karl Deisseroth and Germans Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel.

Like the other Nobels, the economics prize consists of a diploma, a gold medal and a $1.2 million cheque.

The laureates will receive their prizes at formal ceremonies on December 10, the anniversary of Alfred Nobel’s death in 1896.

article_text:
Pakistan expects to achieve its electric vehicle adoption targets ahead of schedule, primarily due to surging oil prices making EVs more economically attractive for consumers.

Amid the growing popularity of electric vehicles (EVs), Pakistan expects to reach its EV adoption target ahead of schedule as consumers increasingly switch from petrol- or diesel-powered cars.

“I feel that the target we had set in our electric-vehicle policy last year, we will achieve it much earlier as the rise in oil prices has brought cost recovery of EVs to one to one-and-a-half year,” Haroon Akhtar, adviser to the prime minister on industries and production, toldBloomberg.

Pakistan has developed policies to promote the adoption of Electric Vehicles (EVs) to reduce its fuel import bill, improve environmental conditions, and foster a sustainable transport system.

In 2019, the government approved the National Electric Vehicles Policy (NEVP) in 2019. The initial goals included EVs making up 30% of all passenger vehicle and heavy-duty truck sales by 2030, and 90% by 2040.

Since the Middle East war started in February, petrol and diesel prices have jumped 54% and 43%, respectively, according to Pakistan State Oil Company Ltd. This has shortened the time it takes for buyers to recoup the higher upfront cost of an EV, Akhtar toldBloomberg.

Oil prices climbed on Thursdayon persistent worries about supply from the key Middle East producing region amid an increase in attacks on shipping in the Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz, while the US cut output as a hurricane menaced offshore production.

Brent crude futures rose $2.28, or 2.28%, to $102.28 a barrel by 0427 GMT. US West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude futures gained $1.66, or 1.88%, to $89.94.

Meanwhile, the official toldBloombergthat the government is also preparing a new auto policy that could be presented to the cabinet within the next two weeks. The government is considering tax incentives for EVs to narrow their price gap with conventional vehicles, Akhtar said.

Last year, theNational Electric Vehicle (NEV) Policy 2025-30was officially launched in June 2025, after being finalised in November 2024 and approved by the Economic Coordination Committee in October 2025.

headline: Fed hikes rates, sees more tightening in search of 'timelier' drop in inflation
summary:
The Federal Reserve, under new chief Kevin Warsh, raised interest rates to combat persistent inflation driven by tariffs, energy costs, and AI spending, with further hikes anticipated.

WASHINGTON: Th...

article_text:
The Federal Reserve, under new chief Kevin Warsh, raised interest rates to combat persistent inflation driven by tariffs, energy costs, and AI spending, with further hikes anticipated.

WASHINGTON: The Federal Reserve raised interest rates on Wednesday and flagged further increases in borrowing costs in coming months, with new US central bank chief Kevin Warsh joining a unanimous decision that effectively acknowledges the Trump administration’s inability so far to control inflation.

While President Donald Trump had promised to lower prices on his watch, the combined impact of his global import tariffs, an energy shock following the start of the US-Israeli war with Iran, and capital spending from the artificial intelligence boom has kept price pressures intense enough that the Fed felt it needed to raise its benchmark overnight interest rate by a quarter of a percentage point to the 3.75%-4.00% range.

New policy projections showed 16 of 18 policymakers anticipate at least one more quarter-percentage-point hike by the end of this year, with only two of them seeing rates remaining stable from here. Warsh apparently again did not submit a rate projection.

It’s the first policy shift under the new Fed chief, who took office in late May after being selected by Trump with an expectation that he would cut rates.

Also read:Fed holds rates steady; three policymakers dissent in favor of a hike

The Fed’s new policy statement and economic projections, to the contrary, show a central bank opening the door on tighter monetary policy through next year, with the policy rate rising to the 4.00%-4.25% range by the end of this year and ending 2027 at the same level.

“Today’s policy action will support a timelier return to the Committee’s 2% goal,” the central bank said in its policy statement after the end of a two-day meeting.

While the statement withheld any forward guidance about coming policy decisions, as is Warsh’s preference, the decision is likely to ease doubts that the Fed chief would hold off on tighter policy out of deference to Trump, a lingering question during his first months in office.

The statement dropped a previous reference attributing current elevated inflation to “supply shocks” particularly in the energy sector, a nod to concerns among policymakers, including Warsh, that price pressures were too broad for comfort.

Warsh is scheduled to hold a press conference beginning at 2:30 p.m. EDT (1830 GMT) to elaborate on the decision.

The rate increase was announced less than two months ahead of midterm elections that will determine whether Trump’s Republicans maintain control of Congress for the final two years of his presidency.

The Republicans are facing an uphill battle with voters angry about gasoline prices that are about a third higher than a year ago and interest rates on home mortgages that have been rising steadily this year. The average rate on a 30-year fixed-rate mortgage is approaching 7%.

Policymakers’ new quarterly economic projections marked up estimates of inflation, as measured by the Personal Consumption Expenditures Price Index, to 3.7% versus the 3.6% projected at the Fed’s June meeting. Inflation is not projected to return to the 2% target until 2029, a year later than previously expected.

Economic growth was marked up slightly from 2.2% to 2.3%, while the unemployment rate is seen ending the year at 4.1%, versus the 4.3% projected in June.

Warsh’s characterization at his press conference of the logic behind the rate increase and the likelihood of further action will be important in shaping the reaction in financial markets that have been raising yields on long-term US Treasury bonds.

The rate hike on Wednesday was widely expected, but investors will be looking for further information from the Fed chief about what might prompt additional increases in borrowing costs.

Warsh has pledged to lower inflation back to 2% “clearly and at sufficient speed” by raising rates as needed.

MILAN: US builder Caddell Construction has formally committed to pay €30.941 ​million ($35.24 million) in a probe into alleged worker exploitation at the site of the new US consulate ‌in Milan, a document seen byReutersshowed.

The Alabama-based construction giant undertook to pay nearly €20 million to workers in overtime, accommodation reimbursements and compensation for non-material damages, according to a document submitted by the firm to Milan prosecutors. It did not admit any liability.

Caddell did not respond to ​a request for comment.

In a statement issued in June, Caddell said it was proactively cooperating with judicial authorities and ​was “committed to treating and paying workers fairly”.

The company specialises in large-scale projects, including contracts for US ⁠embassies and military facilities.

Caddell Construction’s Italian unit was placed under investigation for alleged labour exploitation and put under judicial administration on ​May 29, a measure upheld by a judge two weeks later.

Milan prosecutors and Italy’s Carabinieri police accused the company of recruiting workers ​in India through an intermediary based in New Delhi and employing them on “exhausting shifts, underpaid, without safety protections and under the constant threat of dismissal”.

Iran insists on diplomatic solution after Trump rejects peace plan

The company has also agreed to pay more than €7 million to Italy’s social security agency INPS and almost €4 million to the Labour Inspectorate, the ​document showed.

In the letter to Milan prosecutors, signed by Caddell Construction executive officer Michael Angelo Ranieri and reviewed by Reuters, the ​US company stressed that its commitments did not amount to any admission of wrongdoing.

“Furthermore, they do not imply any acceptance of the legal ‌and factual ⁠assessments made by the authorities involved,” it added.

Case against company set to be dismissed after payment

Two sources with direct knowledge of the matter said the agreement involves the regularisation of around 500 workers, the recognition by the Italian state of residence permits for 270 foreign workers and unemployment benefits for 60 workers who had been dismissed.

One of the two sources said that, once ​the payments had been made, ​Milan prosecutors were expected to ⁠seek the dismissal of the case against Caddell’s Italian unit.

The source added that prosecutors were expected to pursue plea bargain agreements with two Caddell executives arrested as part of the investigation.

Construction ​on the US consulate in Milan started in 2022. The contract was worth almost $210 million ​and work was ⁠initially scheduled to finish in 2025, but this date was subsequently put back to 2028.

A US State Department spokesperson told Reuters in June that US law enforcement was cooperating with the Italian authorities, and that “the US government does not tolerate labour exploitation”.

This is the ⁠latest in ​a series of labour exploitation investigations conducted in recent years by Milan prosecutor Paolo ​Storari.

The probes have forced companies to grant fuller employment rights to more than 60,000 workers and enabled authorities to recover more than €1 billion ($1.1 billion), while also ​fuelling a heated debate over whether Italy’s judiciary is overstepping its role.

article_text:
Four people were killed and dozens injured when 14 coaches of the Rehman Baba Express derailed near Multan, Pakistan, during its journey from Karachi to Peshawar.

At least four passengers were killed and dozens others injured when 14 coaches of the Rehman Baba Express, travelling from Karachi to Peshawar, derailed near Sher Shah railway station in Multan on Tuesday.

According to a Pakistan Railways information officer, initial reports put the number of injured passengers at 30. Rescue 1122, however, reported 53 victims, including four fatalities and 49 injured people.

Rescue 1122 spokesperson Farooq Ahmad toldBusiness Recorderthat 22 of the injured were classified as having minor injuries, while 27 were shifted to medical facilities for treatment. The deceased included three women and one man.

The train was carrying nearly 1,000 passengers at the time of the accident, according to Rescue 1122.

Rescue services received the emergency call at 5:21am and deployed 11 ambulances, three fire vehicles and two rescue vehicles, with 70 rescuers taking part in the operation.

A relief train and a medical van from Multan were dispatched to the accident site. Multan divisional authorities and Rescue 1122 teams were also conducting rescue operations.

The operation was ongoing, according to Rescue 1122.

President, prime minister express concern

President Asif Ali Zardari has expressed concern over the derailment of the Rahman Baba Express near Multan, extending his heartfelt condolences to the families of passengers who lost their lives and wishing a speedy recovery to those injured.

The president directed the relevant authorities to ensure immediate assistance and provide all possible facilities to the affected passengers. He also called for a transparent investigation to determine the cause of the accident.

Meanwhile, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif took notice of the derailment of several coaches of the Rahman Baba Express in Multan and expressed sorrow over the injuries sustained by passengers.

The prime minister directed the authorities concerned to expedite rescue and relief operations and ensure that the injured receive immediate and the best possible medical treatment.

Pakistan has experienced several train accidents this year, with notable incidents resulting in fatalities and injuries, alongside broader concerns about railway safety. Pakistan Railways reported 35 train accidents in the first six months of 2026, though the overall trend showed a decline.

In March, a Lahore-bound Shalimar Express collided with a goods train near Lakha Road Railway Station in Sindh’s Naushahro Feroze district. This incident resulted in one death and 13 injuries. The collision was attributed to the interlocking system being set for a loop line where a goods train was parked, combined with a malfunctioning brake and a red signal.

An internal inspection following this incident revealed that nearly 60% of the Shalimar Express’s coaches were operating without functional brakes, with 10 out of 18 coaches having serious defects, including nine with non-functional brake cylinders.

In another incident in March, multiple bogies of the Tezgam Express, traveling from Rawalpindi to Karachi, derailed near Adam Wahan station in Lodhran. Four bogies overturned, and several others derailed, injuring 25 passengers. The exact cause of this accident was not immediately determined.

A bogie of the Shalimar Express derailed at Khanewal Junction in July while en route from Lahore to Karachi. No casualties or damage were reported, and train services resumed after repairs.

Concerns about frequent train accidents and inadequate security measures were raised by the Senate Standing Committee on Railways in February 2026. The committee noted that disciplinary action had largely focused on train drivers, with senior officers rarely held accountable, and directed the Ministry of Railways to ensure all responsible officials are proceeded against.

The National Assembly Standing Committee on Railways also sought a detailed report on the financial losses from accidents and delays in infrastructure restructuring and safety reforms.

headline: Saudi warning system stayed silent before deadly airport attacks
summary:
Saudi Arabia ceased public warnings of military attacks before deadly Riyadh airport strikes, raising concerns about vulnerability and protection, despite other Gulf nations issuing alerts.

RIYADH: S...
relevant_sector_or_market: APPAREL | COMMERCIAL BANKS | OIL & GAS / ENERGY | OIL & GAS EXPLORATION COMPANIES | PSX / EQUITIES | TECHNOLOGY & COMMUNICATION
article_text:
Saudi Arabia ceased public warnings of military attacks before deadly Riyadh airport strikes, raising concerns about vulnerability and protection, despite other Gulf nations issuing alerts.

RIYADH: Saudi Arabia stopped issuing public warnings of imminent military attacks days before a series of deadly strikes onRiyadh airportthat killed at least 18 people and wounded more than 300.

The government has not said why there were no alerts to the public before the four Riyadh attacks in the past week.

The warnings had served to highlight ​the violence undermining the kingdom’s efforts to project an image of calm to its people and the world during its war withYemen’s Houthis.

Their absence during the airport strikes raised questions about Saudi Arabia’s vulnerability to ‌attack and about its ability to protect residents and visitors, four Western and Arab officials in the region and political analysts told Reuters.

It also reflected efforts to maintain a sense of normalcy, they said.

“They (the Saudi government) want to have it both ways: to launch a military operation and at the same time try to give confidence to the population and external stakeholders,” said Sultan Alamer, a US-based Saudi academic and Senior Resident Fellow at the Middle East Policy Council think tank.

The Saudi civil defence - a national emergency management, rescue and firefighting agency which operates under the interior ministry and issues early warning alerts - and the Saudi ​government media office did not respond to emailed questions on why no alerts were issued.

Saudi Arabia’s approach is also one that some regional analysts said risked backfiring because the absence of warnings has heightened uncertainty in the kingdom.

Riyadh airport to cancel about 60% of flights on Monday after deadly attacks

On Monday, Saudi ​Arabia’s civil defence authority issued its first alerts since September 29, warning of potential threats in Riyadh and southern cities.

Reuterswas unable to ascertain whether the decision to issue alerts again was a response ⁠to the airport attacks, and the Saudi government did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the matter.

All Gulf countries have been hit by Iranian drones and missiles since theUS-Iran warbegan in February, but their governments have handled public ​warnings differently.

Qatar’s interior ministry has issued mobile phone alerts before nearly every attack, including most recent attacks in July, when residents were warned to stay inside and away from windows.

Bahrain and Kuwait have repeatedly sounded sirens urging people to take shelter.

Saudi Arabia began issuing threat alerts ​to mobile phones and social media accounts via a national early warning system in May.

But despite increasing Houthi attacks leading up to last week, the system went silent.

The last alert before last week’s attacks was issued on September 29, for the southern province of Najran, according to posts on the civil defence X account.

The civil defences authority has continued to issue warnings about staying out of harm’s way during adverse weather, including rain and flooding, and did so as recently as Monday.

It also warned residents not to share images, rumours or information about interceptions and impact sites, including in a post on ​Monday, under government regulations issued in March.

Reuters could not determine whether anyone had faced prosecution for sharing such information, and the Saudi government media office did not respond to a request for comment on the matter.

Before last week’s airport attacks, officials from an allied Western ​government asked Saudi authorities why the alerts had stopped, two officials with direct knowledge of the matter said.

The response was that the alerts were too disruptive and many citizens had complained they were being woken by them at night, the officials said.

The Saudi government media office and Saudi officials ‌did not respond ⁠to requests for comment on the assertion.

Former US ambassador to Saudi Arabia Michael Ratney said Riyadh was trying to balance public messaging on attacks with efforts to prevent disruption in the kingdom but had ended up adding to a sense of unease about the strikes.

Riyadh airport to remain shut this week

“Their approach to public messaging seems like a corollary to the quandary they are in: They need to respond to the Houthis but don’t want that to result in societal disruption and their public messaging is a reflection of that,” he said.

“But the lack of alerts of incoming Houthi attacks creates the very nervousness they are trying to avoid.”

Ali Shihabi, a Saudi analyst close to the government, said that with or without early warnings, the kingdom would struggle to defend all of its assets because of its size.

“In Saudi Arabia you have ​too much to protect. It’s a huge country with airports, pipelines ​and oil facilities. There is just not enough coverage to ⁠defend everything at once, not enough Patriots (missile defence systems), interceptors and missile batteries to do it all,” he said.

“Saudi Arabia has an unlimited need for air defences,” he added.“

Despite the attacks, Saudi Arabia hosted an international conference on Monday, though major oil bosses dropped out.

At the World Petroleum Council Energy Congress in Riyadh,Saudi Prince Abdulaziz bin Salaman, a brother of the Saudi crown prince and the kingdom’s energy ​minister, struck a defiant tone while acknowledging risks and Saudi Arabia’s intent to keep its economic plans on track.

He thanked all who had travelled to Riyadh “because you know this country is safe” ​but added:

“Our gathering here does not ⁠mean the risk is gone.” “We will never forfeit any chance to maintain our commitment and our vision,” he said.

Embassies issue their own internal alerts

Despite no public alerts being issued this month until Monday, Riyadh has been attacked about a dozen times, two of the Western officials said.

During that time, Western embassies in the kingdom have been issuing their own internal missile and drone alerts to staff, according to three people familiar with the matter and alerts seen by Reuters.

These internal alerts are compiled from a mixture of US and other Western government intelligence and input from Saudi authorities, ⁠one of those ​people said.

They include alerts sent to staff around the time of two first airport strikes last week according to the people familiar with the matter.

They said that ​even the embassies had received no internal warning before Saturday’s airport strike, without offering an explanation.

One dead in new attack on Saudi airport, a day after Houthi strike kills 13

Reuters could not determine why no warning came before Saturday’s attack, the deadliest of last week’s attacks.

On Sunday, Saudi state TV released footage of Saturday’s strike.

It showed several shots of travellers in the airport terminal. Dozens lined up to board ​a flight. Men and women sat in chairs waiting, their eyes trained on the screens of their mobile phones as they scrolled.

Then, the bright orange flash of a missile explosion.
