article_text:
The Pakistan Textile Council urges the Prime Minister to maintain the Export Facilitation Scheme for all textile inputs, warning that further exclusions of yarns and fabrics will severely harm value-added exports and competitiveness.

The Pakistan Textile Council (PTC) has urged Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif to retain the Export Facilitation Scheme (EFS) for all legitimate export inputs and reject further exclusions of yarns and fabrics, warning that such restrictions could undermine Pakistan’s value-added textile exports.

In a letter to the prime minister, PTC Chairman Fawad Anwar opposed demands to exclude all yarns and fabrics falling under Chapters 52 and 55 of the Pakistan Customs Tariff from the scheme. The council also sent copies of the letter to the Federal Board of Revenue (FBR) chairman and the secretary of commerce.

The council appreciated the government’s efforts to curb misdeclaration and misuse of the EFS but said further exclusions would hurt exporters supplying international markets.

“Accepting these demands would cause serious and lasting harm to Pakistan’s value-added exports,” Anwar said in the letter.

The PTC noted that the government had already removed raw cotton, cotton yarn and grey cloth from the scheme in 2025 through SRO 1359(I)/2025. It said the latest demands contradicted the understanding reached during earlier consultations that no further exclusions would be sought.

Highlighting shifts in global textile demand, the council cited Textile Exchange’s Materials Market Report 2025, which found that synthetic fibres accounted for 69 percent of global fibre production in 2024, while cotton’s share stood at 19 percent.

Man-made fibre (MMF)-based products account for around 63 percent of global textile and apparel trade, compared with approximately 12 percent of Pakistan’s textile and apparel exports, according to the PTC.

The council said competing countries were expanding their presence in the segment, noting that Bangladesh aimed to increase the share of MMF in its apparel exports from around 24 percent to 40 percent by 2030.

Pakistan has almost no domestic viscose or lyocell fibre production, while its polyester value chain faces cost and scale disadvantages compared with Chinese and Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) producers, the letter stated.

As a result, value-added exporters depend on imported MMF yarns and fabrics, many of which are specified by international buyers, to secure and fulfil orders.

The PTC warned that the 2025 exclusions had already forced exporters to pay taxes upfront on affected inputs, increasing liquidity pressures and production costs. Further restrictions on yarns and fabrics under Chapters 52 and 55 could raise input costs, tie up working capital and discourage investment in value-added and MMF-based production capacity.

The council also cautioned that the proposed exclusions could weaken international buyers’ confidence in Pakistan as a reliable sourcing destination.

On concerns about misuse of the scheme, the PTC backed strict action against misdeclaration, under-invoicing and diversion of imports into the domestic market. It said the FBR and Pakistan Customs had the legal powers, systems and personnel to identify and prosecute offenders, adding that recent detections demonstrated the effectiveness of enforcement measures.

“The misuse of a few cannot justify penalising genuine exporters or dismantling a scheme that is central to export competitiveness,” Anwar said.

The council urged the prime minister to ensure that the EFS remained available for all legitimate export inputs, with no further exclusions of yarns and fabrics under Chapters 52 and 55.

It also called for stronger enforcement through input-output coefficient audits, reconciliation of scheme imports with export documents, risk-based examinations and strict penalties for offenders.

Instead of taxing imported inputs, the PTC proposed addressing concerns of domestic suppliers by restoring zero-rating on local supplies of inputs to EFS users.

The council said textiles and apparel remained Pakistan’s largest export sector and that its growth depended on competitive access to the inputs demanded by global markets. It reaffirmed its willingness to work with the government to prevent misuse while protecting legitimate exporters and foreign exchange earnings.

headline: What’s up with McDonald’s latest ad campaign in Pakistan?
summary: The giant billboards as part of McDonald’s latest ad campaign featuring host/actor/comedian Tabish Hashmi front and centre showing how the fast food giant uses local ingredients and contributes billions to Pakistan’s economy had me thinking: what’s up with that?McDonald’s Pakistan is making a concerted pitch about its local roots. Is it simply celebrating 28 years in the country, or is there a bigger reason the brand wants consumers to look beyond the burgers? And could the boycott have something to do with it?The brand wants customers to think about the farmers growing its potatoes and fresh greens, the poultry and dairy partners supplying ingredients, and the network of local businesses that help keep its restaurants running.It is an interesting shift in emphasis. Rather than simply selling the familiar appeal of burgers, fries and Happy Meals, McDonald’s is selling a bigger story: that buying from the brand also supports Pakistani businesses, workers and communities.And it has numbers to back up that argument.The economic contribution pitchAccording to an Oxford Economics study highlighted on McDonald’s Pakistan’sShana Bashana campaign page, the company contributed Rs22.6 billion to Pakistan’s gross domestic product (GDP) and supported an estimated 13,900 jobs. Between July 2024 and June 2025, it spent Rs15.1 billion with Pakistan-based suppliers, representing 91% of its total supplier spend. The company also reports Rs5.9 billion in sustained tax contributions.Its local network includes 55 vendors, covering 29 food suppliers and 26 non-food partners. The local sourcing message is particularly important. McDonald’s is pointing out that its fries do not simply arrive from some distant global supply chain: Pakistani agricultural partners help grow the potatoes used in them. Its campaign also highlights locally sourced greens, poultry and dairy.There is a distinction worth making, however. The 91% figure refers to spending with Pakistan-based suppliers, not to 91% of all ingredients being locally produced. Still, the figures offer a substantive case for the brand’s economic footprint.Is the boycott behind the campaign?McDonald’s has faced boycott calls in Pakistan and other Muslim-majority markets. Images of Israel Defense Forces (IDF) soldiers receiving McDonald’s meals became a major source of controversy. The global company subsequently faced reputational pressure across several markets.Pakistan was no exception. A 2024 news report cited market sources who said McDonald’s and other international fast-food brands had experienced noticeable business declines amid boycott-related consumer sentiment. A 2025 news report also described significant initial sales pressure on McDonald’s and KFC, with some franchises reportedly seeing sales fall by as much as 40%.That is evidence that the boycott had a real commercial impact at the time. It is not evidence that McDonald’s Pakistan is currently experiencing falling sales, though. The company has not publicly provided current local sales figures that would establish whether its business is still suffering.So, is the new campaign an attempt to win customers back? It is a plausible interpretation. If consumers increasingly associate an international brand with a political controversy, reminding them that its local operations support Pakistani farmers and workers offers an alternative way to think about the business.It also gives customers a different consideration: boycotting the brand may affect not only the franchise operator but also local suppliers and employees who depend on its business. That does not settle the ethical debate, but it changes the terms of the conversation.Why emphasise local ingredients now?The local sourcing message may also be a response to a broader change in consumer sentiment. The boycott encouraged some Pakistanis to explore domestic alternatives, from soft drinks to fast food. For an international chain, demonstrating local roots could help counter the perception that choosing a Pakistani alternative is necessarily the more patriotic decision.McDonald’s is effectively arguing that a global brand and a local economic footprint are not mutually exclusive. Its restaurants are locally operated, and its supply chain includes Pakistani businesses. The campaign asks consumers to see those connections as part of the value of the brand.There is also a straightforward marketing explanation. Marking 28 years in Pakistan provides a natural occasion to celebrate suppliers and highlight economic impact. The campaign may be intended to strengthen brand affinity, distinguish McDonald’s from competitors and remind customers why the chain has remained part of the market for nearly three decades.These explanations are not mutually exclusive. A campaign can celebrate genuine local partnerships while also trying to repair a brand’s image and encourage customers to return.The competition is no longer just the other global chainsThere is another factor McDonald’s cannot ignore: Pakistan has developed a much more diverse fast-food market, with local burger businesses offering compelling alternatives.Home-grown chains have helped build a market where consumers have more choices than the familiar international franchises. Independent burger joints and newer local operators can compete through distinctive flavours, generous portions, localised menus, pricing and delivery offers. Reporting during the boycott also documented consumers shifting towards local food businesses.This is not necessarily a story of local brands replacing McDonald’s outright. Global chains retain advantages in brand recognition, consistency, established supply chains and promotions. But the local competition gives customers more reasons to experiment — and more alternatives if they decide not to visit McDonald’s.The result is a tougher question for the brand: what makes it worth choosing over a Pakistani competitor?Its answer appears to be a combination of familiarity, product consistency and now, a stronger story about its contribution to the country.A new story for an old favouriteStill, the timing invites speculation. The boycott may have weakened some consumers’ attachment to the brand, while a stronger local fast-food sector has given them more alternatives. Both could make it more important for McDonald’s to demonstrate why it belongs in Pakistan.What is clear is that McDonald’s wants customers to see more than a global logo: it wants them to see Pakistani farmers, suppliers, employees and businesses behind the meal.Whether that is enough to win back customers who have moved on — for political reasons, better local options or simply changing tastes — remains to be seen.
article_text:
McDonald's Pakistan's new campaign highlights its local sourcing and economic contributions, likely a strategic response to boycotts and growing local competition.

The giant billboards as part of McDonald’s latest ad campaign featuring host/actor/comedian Tabish Hashmi front and centre showing how the fast food giant uses local ingredients and contributes billions to Pakistan’s economy had me thinking: what’s up with that?

McDonald’s Pakistan is making a concerted pitch about its local roots. Is it simply celebrating 28 years in the country, or is there a bigger reason the brand wants consumers to look beyond the burgers? And could the boycott have something to do with it?

The brand wants customers to think about the farmers growing its potatoes and fresh greens, the poultry and dairy partners supplying ingredients, and the network of local businesses that help keep its restaurants running.

It is an interesting shift in emphasis. Rather than simply selling the familiar appeal of burgers, fries and Happy Meals, McDonald’s is selling a bigger story: that buying from the brand also supports Pakistani businesses, workers and communities.

And it has numbers to back up that argument.

According to an Oxford Economics study highlighted on McDonald’s Pakistan’sShana Bashana campaign page, the company contributed Rs22.6 billion to Pakistan’s gross domestic product (GDP) and supported an estimated 13,900 jobs. Between July 2024 and June 2025, it spent Rs15.1 billion with Pakistan-based suppliers, representing 91% of its total supplier spend. The company also reports Rs5.9 billion in sustained tax contributions.

Its local network includes 55 vendors, covering 29 food suppliers and 26 non-food partners. The local sourcing message is particularly important. McDonald’s is pointing out that its fries do not simply arrive from some distant global supply chain: Pakistani agricultural partners help grow the potatoes used in them. Its campaign also highlights locally sourced greens, poultry and dairy.

There is a distinction worth making, however. The 91% figure refers to spending with Pakistan-based suppliers, not to 91% of all ingredients being locally produced. Still, the figures offer a substantive case for the brand’s economic footprint.

McDonald’s has faced boycott calls in Pakistan and other Muslim-majority markets. Images of Israel Defense Forces (IDF) soldiers receiving McDonald’s meals became a major source of controversy. The global company subsequently faced reputational pressure across several markets.

Pakistan was no exception. A 2024 news report cited market sources who said McDonald’s and other international fast-food brands had experienced noticeable business declines amid boycott-related consumer sentiment. A 2025 news report also described significant initial sales pressure on McDonald’s and KFC, with some franchises reportedly seeing sales fall by as much as 40%.

That is evidence that the boycott had a real commercial impact at the time. It is not evidence that McDonald’s Pakistan is currently experiencing falling sales, though. The company has not publicly provided current local sales figures that would establish whether its business is still suffering.

So, is the new campaign an attempt to win customers back? It is a plausible interpretation. If consumers increasingly associate an international brand with a political controversy, reminding them that its local operations support Pakistani farmers and workers offers an alternative way to think about the business.

It also gives customers a different consideration: boycotting the brand may affect not only the franchise operator but also local suppliers and employees who depend on its business. That does not settle the ethical debate, but it changes the terms of the conversation.

The local sourcing message may also be a response to a broader change in consumer sentiment. The boycott encouraged some Pakistanis to explore domestic alternatives, from soft drinks to fast food. For an international chain, demonstrating local roots could help counter the perception that choosing a Pakistani alternative is necessarily the more patriotic decision.

McDonald’s is effectively arguing that a global brand and a local economic footprint are not mutually exclusive. Its restaurants are locally operated, and its supply chain includes Pakistani businesses. The campaign asks consumers to see those connections as part of the value of the brand.

There is also a straightforward marketing explanation. Marking 28 years in Pakistan provides a natural occasion to celebrate suppliers and highlight economic impact. The campaign may be intended to strengthen brand affinity, distinguish McDonald’s from competitors and remind customers why the chain has remained part of the market for nearly three decades.

These explanations are not mutually exclusive. A campaign can celebrate genuine local partnerships while also trying to repair a brand’s image and encourage customers to return.

There is another factor McDonald’s cannot ignore: Pakistan has developed a much more diverse fast-food market, with local burger businesses offering compelling alternatives.

Home-grown chains have helped build a market where consumers have more choices than the familiar international franchises. Independent burger joints and newer local operators can compete through distinctive flavours, generous portions, localised menus, pricing and delivery offers. Reporting during the boycott also documented consumers shifting towards local food businesses.

This is not necessarily a story of local brands replacing McDonald’s outright. Global chains retain advantages in brand recognition, consistency, established supply chains and promotions. But the local competition gives customers more reasons to experiment — and more alternatives if they decide not to visit McDonald’s.

The result is a tougher question for the brand: what makes it worth choosing over a Pakistani competitor?

Its answer appears to be a combination of familiarity, product consistency and now, a stronger story about its contribution to the country.

Still, the timing invites speculation. The boycott may have weakened some consumers’ attachment to the brand, while a stronger local fast-food sector has given them more alternatives. Both could make it more important for McDonald’s to demonstrate why it belongs in Pakistan.

What is clear is that McDonald’s wants customers to see more than a global logo: it wants them to see Pakistani farmers, suppliers, employees and businesses behind the meal.

Whether that is enough to win back customers who have moved on — for political reasons, better local options or simply changing tastes — remains to be seen.

headline: Pakistan car sales rise 43% in Q1 FY2026-27
summary: Car sales in Pakistan rose 43% year-on-year in the first quarter of FY2026-27, with analysts attributing the hike to an improving macroeconomic environment that boosted vehicle demand.Car sales surged by 43% to 41,872 units, while sales of jeeps and pickups decreased by 34% to 8,608 units in July-September 2026. Sales of trucks increased by 53% to 2,516 units.However, sales of buses went down 5% to 211 units.  Moreover, sales of farm tractors also went up by 38% to 4,109 units.Sales of two- and three-wheelers, including motorbikes and rickshaws, increased by 28% to 553,994 units, according to Pakistan Automotive Manufacturers Association (PAMA) data released on Tuesday evening.Car sales declined by nearly 10% from 12,126 units in September 2025 to 10,939 units in September 2026.Speaking about automotive production and sales figures during the first quarter of FY27, PAMA director general Razi-ur-Rahman said in a statement, “This renewed sales momentum is on the back of easing of inflationary pressures and an improving macroeconomic environment. During the first quarter of FY27, the industry has experienced varying trajectories across segments.”“While overall industry volumes are steadily recovering, there is perceptible hesitation on part of the players in the market. The Original Equipment Manufacturers (OEMs) as well as the buyers are hesitant to take investment decisions. The lack of clarity about the auto policy continues to dominate the market sentiment,” he said.
article_text:
Pakistan's car sales surged 43% in Q1 FY2026-27, driven by an improving economy and easing inflation, despite some segment declines and market hesitation.

Car sales in Pakistan rose 43% year-on-year in the first quarter of FY2026-27, with analysts attributing the hike to an improving macroeconomic environment that boosted vehicle demand.

Car sales surged by 43% to 41,872 units, while sales of jeeps and pickups decreased by 34% to 8,608 units in July-September 2026. Sales of trucks increased by 53% to 2,516 units.

However, sales of buses went down 5% to 211 units.  Moreover, sales of farm tractors also went up by 38% to 4,109 units.

Sales of two- and three-wheelers, including motorbikes and rickshaws, increased by 28% to 553,994 units, according to Pakistan Automotive Manufacturers Association (PAMA) data released on Tuesday evening.

Car sales declined by nearly 10% from 12,126 units in September 2025 to 10,939 units in September 2026.

Speaking about automotive production and sales figures during the first quarter of FY27, PAMA director general Razi-ur-Rahman said in a statement, “This renewed sales momentum is on the back of easing of inflationary pressures and an improving macroeconomic environment. “While overall industry volumes are steadily recovering, there is perceptible hesitation on part of the players in the market. The lack of clarity about the auto policy continues to dominate the market sentiment,” he said.

article_text:
Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif said on Tuesday that wheat was available in abundant quantities to meet domestic needs, while vowing no leniency for hoarders, according to the Prime Minister’s Office (PMO).

PM Shehbaz chaired the first National Agricultural and Food Security Council (NAFSC) meeting in Islamabad today, according to a statement issued by the PMO.

Addressing the meeting, the prime minister said that wheat was available in abundant quantities to meet domestic needs.

“No leniency will be shown to those hoarding wheat,” PM Shehbaz was quoted as saying. “It is essential to determine the fair price of wheat before sowing so that farmers receive appropriate compensation for their labour.”

“We want farmers to get the fair price for wheat and for consumers to have affordable wheat,” he added.

The premier stated that the decision regarding the price of wheat would be made in consultation with the provinces.

“The consultation with the provinces will be completed soon, and the price of wheat will be announced shortly,” he said.

The prime minister further termed agriculture the “backbone of the national economy” and said it could set Pakistan’s economy on the path to growth in the short term, the PMO added.

Punjab Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz, Sindh Food Minister Makhdoom Mehboob uz Zaman, and relevant senior officials also participated in the meeting, according to the statement.

During the meeting, the prime minister commended CM Maryam for “taking commendable steps such as farmers’ development, aquaculture, shrimp farming, and providing direct subsidies to farmers through the Kisan Card”.

The Sindh chief minister was also “working day and night for the development of farmers and providing them with facilities”, PM Shehbaz said, according to the statement.

The prime minister noted that the livestock sector also had vast potential to increase national exports, noting that measures were being taken to boost exports of Pakistani halal meat.

He added that the federal government would “provide all kinds of support to the provinces for the development of agriculture”.

“Providing fertilisers, quality seeds, modern machinery, and equipment and technical capabilities for better water utilisation to farmers at low cost is the top priority,” the prime minister said.

He added that ensuring fair prices to farmers for their crops, particularly small and medium-scale farmers, was a priority as well.

The Punjab chief minister and Sindh food minister shed light on the measures taken by the provincial governments for the development of farmers in their provinces, the PMO said.

It added that the briefings were also given at the meeting on measures for the development of agriculture in Balochistan, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Azad Jammu and Kashmir, and Gilgit-Baltistan.

Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar, federal ministers Rana Tanveer Hussain, Dr Musadiq Malik, Jam Kamal Khan, Ahad Khan Cheema, Ahsan Iqbal, Attaullah Tarar, Khalid Hussain Magsi and Mian Moin Wattoo; and advisors Rana Sanaullah and Haroon Akhtar were among those who attended the meeting, according to the PMO.

In a meeting last week, National Food Security Minister Rana Tanveer Hussain said the targets for Rabi crops would befinalisedafter the “announcement of an illustrative price for wheat”.

“We are conscious of the challenges faced by our farmers due to rising input, energy and transportation costs,” the minister said.

Last month, the Pakistan Kissan Ittehaddemandeda Rs5,000 per 40kg support price for wheat, warning that farmers may not sow wheat for the next season if the government delays announcing crop policies.

The association had maintained that the farmers were unable to afford balanced fertiliser use because they were not recovering production costs.

In Sindh, Chief Minister Murad Ali Shahapprovedthe release of government wheat at the rate of Rs12,500 per 100kg bag from Oct 15 in order to stabilise flour prices and ensure its availability in the province.

Meanwhile, Punjab CM Maryam called an emergency meeting in response to rising flour prices, expressing strong displeasure over the increase, according to a PML-N post on X.

“The chief minister directed that affordable flour and wheat must be provided to the public under all circumstances,” the post said.

It added that a decision was made to increase the government-subsidised wheat quota for flour mills.

A subsidy of Rs10 billion was approved to ensure the availability of affordable flour, the PML-N said.

Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif briefed allied parties on constitutional measures taken in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa to address security, economic stability, and terrorism, criticizing the PTI provincial government's failures.

Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif on Tuesday briefed a parliamentary delegation of allied political parties on the situation in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (KP), saying constitutional measures were taken after consultations within the federal cabinet to address security concerns and safeguard economic stability.

According to a press release issued by the Prime Minister’s Office, Shehbaz said a non-partisan technocratic advisory council had been established to assist the governor in improving law and order, strengthening the economy and eliminating terrorism in the province.

The prime minister said the conduct of the Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI)-led provincial government and its failure to adopt an unequivocal stance against terrorism had posed risks to Pakistan’s growing economy.

He said the federal cabinet had decided, through mutual consultation, to take constitutional measures under Articles 232 and 234 of the Constitution.

Shehbaz alleged that the KP government had neither clearly condemned terrorism nor taken decisive action against terrorists.

He said members of the armed forces, security agencies and police had sacrificed their lives over the past several years to protect the country and maintain peace in the province.

The prime minister further criticised the PTI and its provincial government, saying that over the past 13 years they had failed to deliver adequate public welfare and ensure the safety of citizens’ lives and property.

He said the federal government had provided more than Rs800 billion to KP under the National Finance Commission (NFC) framework to support efforts to eliminate terrorism.

However, he alleged, the provincial government had failed to take effective measures to strengthen the Counter Terrorism Department (CTD) and establish Safe City projects.

The parliamentary delegation included representatives of the Balochistan Awami Party (BAP), Pakistan Muslim League-Quaid (PML-Q), Istehkam-e-Pakistan Party (IPP) and Pakistan Muslim League-Zia (PML-Z).

The delegation assured the prime minister that allied parties stood with the federal government in the current situation and praised his leadership for guiding the country through difficult circumstances.

The delegation also said KP’s residents had been deprived of development in health, education and infrastructure during the PTI’s 13-year rule. It expressed confidence that, with federal government support, the province would join the country’s broader path towards development and prosperity.

Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar, Defence Minister Khawaja Asif, Law and Justice Minister Azam Nazeer Tarar, Parliamentary Affairs Minister Tariq Fazal Chaudhry, and the prime minister’s adviser on political affairs and inter-provincial coordination, Rana Sanaullah, also attended the meeting.

The SBP has halted sugar exports from Khyber Pakhtunkhwa mills, awaiting provincial government endorsement, while Punjab and Sindh mills can proceed with their revised export quotas.

The State Bank of Pakistan (SBP) directed commercial banks on Tuesday to put sugar exports by the mills located in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa’s (KP) on hold till the provincial administration endorses the overseas sales of the commodity.

In a circular titled ‘Revised Instructions - Export of 200,000 MT [Metric Ton] of Sugar’, the central bank asked commercial banks to process export transaction of the commodity by eligible sugar mills located in Punjab and Sindh after the two provincial governments endorsed the revised quotas of sugar mills located in their respective territories.

“The Government of Punjab and Government of Sindh have endorsed the revised quotas of sugar mills located in their respective provinces. The endorsement from the Government of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (KP) is still awaited. Accordingly, authorised dealers [commercial banks] may process the export transactions of eligible sugar mills of Punjab and Sindh as per their revised quotas, subject to [applicable] conditions,” according to the circular.

“The endorsement of revised quota by the Government of KP will be communicated as and when received from MNFSR [Ministry of National Food Security & Research]. Accordingly, the authorised dealers shall process export transactions of eligible sugar mills located in KP after receipt of this confirmation.”

SBP said the MNFSR on October 09, 2026 had communicated the revised province and mill-wise sugar export quotas received from Pakistan Sugar Mills Association (PSMA), along with the correction to the names of three sugar mills.

Earlier in September 2026, the Economic Coordination Committee (ECC) of the Cabinet allowed export of 200,000 MT of sugar with certain terms and conditions. The ECC’s decision has also been ratified by the Federal Cabinet.

The government on Tuesday reduced the price of petrol by Rs2.71 per litre, and that of high-speed diesel (HSD) by Rs0.03 per litre.

Following the revision, petrol will retail at Rs392.66 per litre, while HSD will cost Rs396.82 per litre. The government continues to levy Rs114 per litre in taxes and duties on petrol and Rs100 per litre on diesel.

According to the Petroleum Division’s notification, the new prices are applicable for Oct 14 (Wednesday).

The price of HSD has come down from apeak of Rs520.35recorded on April 3. Its price had started rising from Rs281 per litre after the US-Iran war broke out on February 28.

The petrol price hadpeaked at Rs458.41on April 3 after beginning itsupward trajectoryfrom Rs266 in the first week of March.

Meanwhile, the government hasreintroduceda raft of austerity measures in response to rising fuel prices amid the ongoing Middle East conflict. Under these measures, markets are required to close by 9pm and fuel allocations for official vehicles has been cut by 50 per cent for three months.

On September 13, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif also announced a “relief scheme” for users of motorcycles, autos and vehicles of up to 800cc to “alleviate the burden” of rising global oil prices.

Previously, on July 17, Petroleum Minister Ali Pervaiz Malikannouncedthat fuel prices would now be fixed on a daily basis due to fluctuations in international market prices following renewed hostilities between Iran and the US.

Prior to this, the government had been announcingweekly revisionsto fuel prices since early March, alongside measures for the conservation of fuel amid possible oil supply disruptions due to the ongoing conflict in the Middle East. The federal government in April alsoannouncedtargeted relief measures to provide subsidised fuel.

The petroleum minister stated that the cabinet and the prime minister had decided to give the Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority (Ogra) the responsibility of deciding fuel prices on a daily basis based on international market trends.

Petrol is mainly used in private transport, small vehicles, rickshaws and two-wheelers, and changes in its price affect the middle and lower-middle classes.

Similarly, changes in diesel prices also impact the public at large, as it is mainly used in the heavy transport sector, power plants and large generators.

Petrol and high-speed diesel (HSD) are the major revenue earners, with monthly sales of about 700,000 to 800,000 tonnes, compared to just 10,000 tonnes of monthly demand for kerosene.

ISLAMABAD: European Union Commissioner for Internal Affairs and Migration Magnus Brunner called on Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif on Tuesday to discuss strengthening Pakistan-EU cooperation in migration and mobility, one of the eight pillars of thePakistan-EU Strategic Engagement Plan 2019.

Welcoming Commissioner Brunner on his first visit to Pakistan, the prime minister underscored the importance Pakistan attaches to its partnership with the EU, according to a press release by the Prime Minister’s Office (PMO).

The premier highlighted Pakistan’s sustained efforts to curb irregular migration and combat migrant smuggling and human trafficking through legislative reforms, institutional strengthening, effective enforcement and international cooperation.

He reaffirmed Pakistan’s commitment to further strengthening cooperation across all pillars of the Pakistan-EU Strategic Engagement Plan.

PM Shehbaz emphasised that efforts to address irregular migration should be complemented by practical opportunities for safe, orderly and regular migration.

He noted that expanding legal pathways for Pakistani skilled workers and professionals would help meet the labour market needs of European countries while reducing prospective migrants’ vulnerability to smuggling networks.

Brunner appreciated the measures taken and cooperation extended by the government of Pakistan, the PMO said.

He expressed confidence that these efforts would contribute to expanding legal migration pathways and promoting mutually beneficial labour mobility between Pakistan and the European Union.

Brunner also called on President Asif Ali Zardari at the President’s House today, according to a two-part statement issued by the official presidential account on social media.

“The meeting focused on Pakistan-EU relations, cooperation on migration management, efforts to combat human trafficking and migrant smuggling, and opportunities to facilitate legal migration,” the statement said.

President Zardari called for greater opportunities for legal migration for Pakistani workers and professionals in Europe. He emphasised that Pakistan’s sustained efforts to curb irregular migration should be matched by “expanded legal pathways, skills-based mobility and structured cooperation” with the EU.

He said that Pakistan attached great importance to its cooperation with the EU and reaffirmed the country’s commitment to implementing the Pakistan-EU Strategic Engagement Plan.

The president highlighted the cooperation between the two countries in curbing irregular migration, noting that Pakistan continued to implement the EU Readmission Agreement and had readmitted more than 30,000 individuals over the years. He stressed the country’s commitment to combating human trafficking and irregular migration through “stronger legislation, institutional capacity, border controls and international cooperation”, the statement said.

The president noted that, according to EU figures, irregular migration from Pakistan reduced by 64 per cent in the last 18 months, making it the only country in the region to achieve such a reduction. He said this progress reflected Pakistan’s “sustained efforts” and underlined the importance of expanding safe and legal avenues for migration.

According to the president’s office, the meeting was informed that Pakistan had sought the EU’s assistance in strengthening the capacity of the Pakistan Coast Guards and the Federal Investigation Agency (FIA) to enhance efforts to combat irregular migration and migrant smuggling.

“The president emphasised that legal migration pathways are essential to providing safe opportunities for workers and reducing reliance on smuggling networks,” the statement added.

He highlighted the Pakistan-EU Migration and Mobility Dialogue as a “useful framework for matching Pakistan’s human-resource potential with European labour-market needs”, and expressed the hope that the next round of dialogue — expected to take place in Brussels early next year — would advance this cooperation.

He expressed the country’s readiness to work with the EU on a structured mechanism to match its workforce with European labour-market requirements.

President Zardari also welcomed the expansion of the EU Talent Partnerships framework and called for greater opportunities for skilled workers and professionals, including through circular migration.

He expressed the hope that, given this partnership and the country’s efforts to curb irregular migration, the EU would consider establishing a European Legal Gateway Office in Pakistan.

He said Pakistan and the EU have a “broad-based relationship spanning political dialogue, trade, development cooperation and other areas of mutual interest”, the statement added. He expressed confidence that continued engagement would strengthen mutual understanding and help advance practical cooperation on migration and mobility.

Commissioner Brunner appreciated Pakistan’s role in maintaining regional balance and said Pakistan has done an “amazing job” in this regard, the statement noted.

He also commended Pakistan’s efforts to prevent irregular migrants from undertaking dangerous journeys that cost many of them their lives.

The commissioner was accompanied by EU Ambassador to Pakistan Raimundas Karoblis; Director for Migration and Home Affairs of the European Commission Henrik Nielsen; and member of Brunner’s cabinet, Grigorios Delavekouras.

Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi, Minister of State for Interior Talal Chaudhry, Senator Sherry Rehman, Senator Saleem Mandviwalla and former federal minister Naveed Qamar also attended the meeting, the statement added.

The EU commissioner also met with Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar in Islamabad, during which the deputy premier highlighted Pakistan’s efforts to curb irregular migration and combat migrant smuggling and human trafficking, the Foreign Office (FO) said.

He stressed that these efforts should be complemented by greater opportunities for legal migration for Pakistani skilled workers and professionals.

According to a statement issued by the FO, Dar expressed satisfaction with the positive momentum in Pakistan–EU relations.

“The two sides discussed ways to strengthen cooperation on migration and mobility, a key pillar of the Pakistan–EU Strategic Engagement Plan (2019),” the FO said.

It added that Brunner appreciated Pakistan’s progress in curbing irregular migration and noted the scope for expanding legal pathways for migration.

Dar reaffirmed Pakistan’s commitment to further strengthening its partnership with the EU. He expressed the hope that Brunner’s visit would lead to “practical outcomes that benefit both sides”, the statement added.

Separately, Brunner also met with Interior Minister Naqvi in Islamabad, where they discussed enhancing cooperation in border security, legal migration and border management.

The meeting was followed by delegation-level talks.

Brunner appreciated Pakistan’s measures against illegal migration, describing the 64pc reduction in illegal migration to Europe resulting from the country’s efforts as commendable.

He said the Federal Investigation Agency (FIA) had demonstrated professional competence despite limited resources, which was commendable. He added that the decline in illegal migration would pave the way for legal migration.

Naqvi said Pakistan had adopted a zero-tolerance policy towards illegal migration.

“After a 64pc reduction in illegal migration, our next target is its complete elimination,” the interior minister said, describing illegal migration as a serious global issue.

The two sides also discussed the promotion of legal migration and enhancing opportunities for skilled workers between Pakistan and the European Union.

Both sides agreed to further strengthen cooperation in immigration, institutional coordination and border management, and to work together on the EU’s Eastern Corridor Initiative to eliminate illegal migration.

They also discussed increasing mutual cooperation to enhance the capacity of Pakistan Coast Guards and agreed to increase collaboration to promote border security and legal migration.

Brunner assured Pakistan of all possible cooperation in this regard.

The meeting was attended by the interior secretary, special and additional interior secretaries, FIA director general, Federal Constabulary inspector general, NCCIA director general, passports director general, Islamabad chief commissioner and other officials.

Last month, Naqvi said Pakistan had recorded a64pc reductionin illegal migration to Europe, describing the achievement as challenging despite limited resources.

He said Pakistan’s next target was to eliminate illegal migration completely, stressing the need to expand legal migration opportunities, adopt modern technology and strengthen institutional capacity.

In February, Pakistan and three European countries — Italy, Spain and Greece — reached aconsensuson promoting legal pathways to “effectively combat illegal migration”. The three countries endorsed Naqvi’s proposal to establish legal pathways as a strategy to combat illegal migration and human smuggling during a conference.

article_text:
The Pakistan Stock Exchange's KSE-100 Index fell 348 points due to persistent selling pressure and cautious investor sentiment, amidst rising inflation projections and global market volatility.

Selling pressure continued at the Pakistan Stock Exchange (PSX) on Tuesday, with the benchmark KSE-100 Index closing 348 points lower amid bearish sentiment.

The KSE-100 Index witnessed some buying in the first half, hitting an intra-day high of 166,070.48. However, selling returned to the bourse, pushing the benchmark index to an intra-day low of 164,773.67.

At close, the KSE-100 Index settled at 164,776.44, down 347.97 points or 0.21%.

“The benchmark remained range-bound throughout the session, trading between 164,774 and 166,070, reflecting cautious investor sentiment and persistent selling pressure in index-heavy stocks,” brokerage house Topline Securities said in its post-market report.

“Investor sentiment is likely to remain cautious amid ongoing market volatility. Near-term market direction will depend on developments in key economic indicators, institutional activity, and investor positioning. Selective opportunities may emerge in fundamentally sound stocks, while a prudent investment approach remains advisable.”

Index-heavy stocks remained under pressure, with PTC, UBL, HBL, LUCK, and MARI emerging as the major laggards. Collectively, these stocks contributed approximately 343 points to the index’s decline, weighing on overall market performance, Topline said.

Pakistan’s inflation rate is projectedto rise to 9.9% in 2027, while economic growth is expected to ease to 3.5%, according to data released by the International Monetary Fund’s (IMF)World Economic Outlook (WEO)released on Tuesday.

The IMF data showed inflation at 7.1% in 2026, up from 4.5% in 2025. Pakistan’s gross domestic product (GDP) growth is projected at 3.6% in 2026, compared with 3.2% in 2025, before moderating to 3.5% in 2027.

As the government seeks to diversify its funding sources, Pakistan plans to return to China’s domestic bond market for further yuan-denominated borrowing and is exploring the possibility of issuing yen-denominated bonds in Japan,Finance Minister Muhammad Aurangzeb said in an interview toNikkie Asia.

Pakistanissued its first panda bond worth 1.75 billion yuan($261 million) in mid-May under a 7.2-billion-yuan programme, with partial guarantees from the Asian Development Bank and the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank.

SE Fruits and Vegetable Limitedwill withdraw its existing initial public offering (IPO) application and submit a fresh one with additional disclosures about the transition of its underlying business from a partnership to a public limited company, the company said.

“The Board of Directors of SE Fruits and Vegetable Limited has decided to withdraw the Company’s current IPO application and submit a fresh application after incorporating additional disclosures into the prospectus,” the company said in a statement.

On Monday,the PSX witnessed heavy selling as domestic political uncertainty following the imposition of emergency and governor rule in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, coupled with regional geopolitical tensions involving Saudi Arabia, the Houthis, the United States and Iran, prompted investors to reduce their equity exposure. The KSE-100 Index plunged by 1,964.87 points, or 1.18%, to close at 165,124.41 points.

Internationally,Asian equities fell sharply on Tuesdayled ​by technology shares as a widening conflict in the Middle East kept oil prices elevated, supporting the dollar ‌ahead of an earnings season that will set the tone for the rest of the year.

Energy prices are back driving global markets as investors weigh the geopolitical developments in the Middle East and Russia-Ukraine, with Brent crude futures at $105.9 per barrel, near a two-week high.

In stocks, MSCI’s broadest index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan fell ​2% in early trading, with tech-heavy South Korea’s KOSPI sliding 6%. Japan’s Nikkei sank 2.6% after returning from a holiday.

Overnight, the tech-heavy ​Nasdaq fell 0.5%, dragged by chipmakers as investors fret about the durability of the rally in AI stocks amid higher competition ​between the US and China.

The cautious sentiment helped keep the US dollar near an 18-month high. The euro last bought $1.1157, while the Japanese yen was at 158.50 per US dollar.

Investors’ attention will be on the slew of US bank earnings this week to get a gauge on the impact of the recent surge in Treasury yields on dealmaking, lending growth and funding costs ​across the industry.

A toxic mix of ​inflationary pressure from elevated energy ⁠prices and worries about ballooning government debt have triggered several bouts of bond selloffs in recent weeks, pushing borrowing costs to multi-decade highs across the globe.

Four of the six largest US lenders, JPMorgan ​Chase, Goldman Sachs, Citigroup and Wells Fargo will report results later in the day.

Meanwhile,the Pakistani rupee extendedits marginal gains against the US dollar in the inter-bank market on Tuesday. The local unit closed the day at 276.96, a gain of Re0.01 against the greenback.

Volume on the all-share index increased to 383.75 million from 362.95 million recorded in the previous close.

The value of shares declined to Rs13.10 billion from Rs14.51 billion in the previous session.

LSE Financial(R) was the volume leader with 32.28 million shares, followed by Waves Home App with 21.85 million shares, and WorldCall Telecom with 19.53 million shares.

Shares of 500 companies were traded on Tuesday, of which 223 registered an increase, 226 recorded a fall, and 51 remained unchanged.
